title: Does This Gradient Spark Joy?
claim: Our gated method matches the full-compute baseline in learning quality while using a tiny fraction of the expensive computation, beating the standard baseline.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, same y-axis with different x-axis cost measures
description: Two line plots sit side by side with a shared log-scaled y-axis, classification error from 1 down to about 0.02. Each plot has three curves with shaded standard-error bands: PG in blue, DG in red, and DG-K, the Kondo gate, in green. A legend titled 'alg' sits to the right of each plot. The left plot has forward passes (M) on the x-axis. There the red and green curves fall close together well below the blue one. The right plot has backward passes (M) on the x-axis. There the green curve drops almost vertically near zero, far to the left of the red and blue curves. The captions beneath read '(a) Forward passes: DG-K ≈ DG ≫ PG' and '(b) Backward passes: DG-K ≫ DG ≫ PG'. The eye goes first to the steep green line in the right panel.
caption: PG, DG, and Kondo gate (DG-K) at $\rho = 0.03$ on MNIST. (a) The Kondo gate matches DG despite computing 3% of backward passes. (b) It dominates by two orders of magnitude in backward-pass space. Averaged over 30 seeds; shading shows $\pm 1$ standard error.
abstract: Policy gradient computes a backward pass for every sample, although the backward pass is expensive and most samples carry little learning value. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) scores learning value in the forward pass with \emph{delight}, the product of advantage and surprisal (negative log-probability). We introduce the \emph{Kondo gate}, which compares delight against a compute price and pays for a backward pass only when the sample is worth it; sweeping the price traces a quality--cost trade-off. On MNIST, keeping 3\% of gradient terms learns faster than standard policy gradient even when backward passes are free, and nearly matches full DG. In bandits, zero-price gating preserves the expected gradient direction and removes its perpendicular noise, delight ranks samples more reliably than additive mixes of value and surprise, and a rare action with high reward variance marks where delight fails. On transformer token reversal, the gate's advantage grows with sequence length and vocabulary size. Because delight tolerates moderate noise, a cheap approximate forward pass could screen samples before expensive backpropagation, a training analogue of speculative decoding.
